citations.quote: A data type tsvector is provided for storing preprocessed documents, along with a type tsquery for representing processed queries

questions.notes: Content verified. The staged source_ref points at the chapter landing page; the exact rules are in the 12.1 subsections, cited here. tsvector stores preprocessed lexemes; tsquery represents the query.

citations.quote: Searching and ranking are performed entirely on the tsvector representation of a document
Full text searching in PostgreSQL is based on the match operator @@

questions.notes: Content verified. The staged source_ref points at the chapter landing page; the exact rules are in the 12.1 subsections, cited here. Essay key correctly covers normalization/stemming, @@ matching and why a leading-wildcard LIKE is weaker.

citations.quote: plainto_tsquery transforms the unformatted text querytext to a tsquery value.
phraseto_tsquery behaves much like plainto_tsquery , except that it inserts the <-> (FOLLOWED BY) operator between surviving words instead of the & (AND) operator.

questions.notes: Content verified. The staged source_ref points at the chapter landing page; the exact rules are in the 12.1 subsections, cited here. plainto uses & (AND anywhere); phraseto uses <-> (adjacent and ordered).

citations.quote: Searching for phrases is possible with the help of the <-> (FOLLOWED BY) tsquery operator, which matches only if its arguments have matches that are adjacent and in the given order.

questions.notes: Content verified. The staged source_ref points at the chapter landing page; the exact rules are in the 12.1 subsections, cited here. <-> requires adjacency in the given order.

citations.quote: OR : the word “ or ” will be converted to the | operator.
! (NOT) binds most tightly, <-> (FOLLOWED BY) next most tightly, then & (AND), with | (OR) binding the least tightly.

questions.notes: Content verified. The staged source_ref points at the chapter landing page; the exact rules are in the 12.1 subsections, cited here. websearch maps '-' to ! and 'or' to |; ! binds tightest, then <->, then &, then |, so the parsed query is database OR (network AND NOT nosql).

citations.quote: Rounds to nearest integer. For numeric , ties are broken by rounding away from zero.

questions.notes: numeric round(-1.7) = -2 (nearest), trunc(-1.7) = -1 (toward zero).

citations.quote: mod ( y numeric_type , x numeric_type ) → numeric_type

questions.notes: Integer / integer truncates; casting an operand to numeric yields 3.5.

citations.quote: Remainder of y / x ; available for smallint , integer , bigint , and numeric

questions.notes: mod(-7,3) = -1: the remainder takes the sign of the dividend.

citations.quote: Concatenates the text representations of all the arguments. NULL arguments are ignored.

questions.notes: || propagates NULL; concat ignores NULL arguments and returns 'AnLe'.

citations.quote: char_length('josé') → 4

questions.notes: Source value is U+00E9 (é), one character and two UTF-8 bytes; char_length 1, octet_length 2. Verified at the byte level, not from console rendering.

citations.quote: To match a literal underscore or percent sign without matching other characters, the respective character in pattern must be preceded by the escape character.

questions.notes: Underscore is a single-character wildcard; ESCAPE makes it literal.

citations.quote: LIKE pattern matching always covers the entire string.

questions.notes: LIKE covers the whole string; ~ searches anywhere unless anchored; ILIKE is case-insensitive.

citations.quote: date + integer → date

questions.notes: date + integer advances by days and honors leap-year calendar rules (2024-02-29 exists).

citations.quote: A domain is a user-defined data type that is based on another underlying type . Optionally, it can have constraints that restrict its valid values to a subset of what the underlying type would allow.
the main purpose of a collation is to set LC_COLLATE , which controls the sort order.

questions.notes: Domain is a reusable named type with constraints applied to every column; collation controls comparison/sort. Both consequences are correct.

citations.quote: Unique prefixes of these strings are also accepted, for example t or n .

questions.notes: Accepted true spellings are true/yes/on/1 and their unique prefixes; 'enable' is not accepted.

citations.quote: Values of type character are physically padded with spaces to the specified width n , and are stored and displayed that way.

questions.notes: char(n) is blank-padded but trailing spaces are insignificant in comparison; varchar(n) does not pad.

citations.quote: For double precision , the tie-breaking behavior is platform dependent, but “ round to nearest even ” is the most common rule.

questions.notes: numeric rounds ties away from zero (2.5 -> 3); float8 rounds ties to nearest even (2.5 -> 2).

citations.quote: date - date → integer

questions.notes: date - date returns integer days; 2024 is a leap year so February has 29 days.

citations.quote: Returns true if all non-null input values are true, otherwise false.

questions.notes: bool_and/bool_or ignore NULL; with TRUE and NULL inputs both return TRUE. All-NULL input would return NULL.

citations.quote: Trailing spaces are removed when converting a character value to one of the other string types.

questions.notes: Trailing char(n) padding is removed when converting to text for ||, so the result is 'abcd'.

citations.quote: Assigning a value of the underlying type to a field or variable of the domain type is allowed without writing an explicit cast, but the domain's constraints will be checked.

questions.notes: Domain CHECK applies to every column of the domain; casting to the base type drops the constraint.

citations.quote: Is subnet strictly contained by subnet?

questions.notes: << tests strict subnet containment and >> is its reverse; a /32 host address is contained in /24, so both are TRUE.
